teaser: For decades a museum label hid her name. A niece in Los Angeles got it back.

lesson.text: In the 1940s this painting hung in a Vienna museum under a new label: “Lady in Gold”. No name. The woman it shows, Adele Bloch-Bauer, was Jewish, and the Nazis who had taken the picture from her family's home preferred that nobody be reminded of it.

Gustav Klimt had died in 1918, Adele in 1925. Her husband Ferdinand, a sugar manufacturer, fled Austria in 1938 when Nazi Germany annexed the country, and lost his factory, his house and his art. After the war the portrait stayed in Vienna's Belvedere museum for sixty years. Printed on posters and souvenirs, it became a kind of Austrian Mona Lisa.

In 1998 Adele's niece Maria Altmann, who had escaped Vienna as a young bride and run a dress shop in Los Angeles, asked for the painting back. Her case against Austria went as far as the U.S. Supreme Court. An Austrian panel finally ruled in her favor in 2006. She was eighty-nine.

Months later the cosmetics heir Ronald Lauder bought the portrait for the Neue Galerie, his museum in New York, for a reported 135 million dollars. No painting was known to have sold for more at the time. So what is it about this square of gold? Begin with the few parts that are not gold at all.
Find the woman inside the pattern.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Heavy eyelids, flushed cheeks, parted lips under a cloud of dark hair. Klimt paints her in oils with soft, lifelike shading, like a photograph set into a jewel.

spots.title: The hands
spots.text: Her hands fold over each other at an awkward angle. Adele is said to have had a crooked finger that she liked to hide. Klimt keeps the nervous gesture instead of tidying it.

spots.title: The choker
spots.text: A wide collar of jewels, tight around the throat. It was a real necklace. Years later it was given to Maria Altmann as a wedding present, and in 1938 the Nazis took it too.

lesson.text: Face, shoulders, hands: that is all the skin there is, a small island in the upper right. Everything else is flattened into ornament. You cannot tell where the dress stops and the armchair begins, or how far away the wall is. A living person seems to be dissolving into a precious object.

The shimmer is real metal. Klimt laid gold leaf and silver leaf, sheets of metal beaten thinner than paper, onto the canvas, then painted over them and pressed patterns into them. He had grown up around the craft: his father was a gold engraver.

In 1903 Klimt traveled to Ravenna, in Italy, and stood before church mosaics some 1,400 years old, where a Byzantine empress and her court glitter against walls of gold. He wrote home that their splendor was beyond belief. Adele's portrait was ordered that same year.

It took him four years and more than a hundred preparatory drawings. Finished in 1907, the portrait marks the height of what is called his Golden Phase. Klimt had led the Vienna Secession, a group of artists who walked out of the city's official art society in 1897 to bring painting, design and craft together. Here a portrait turns into goldsmith's work.

The patterns are not random filling. Klimt borrowed signs from ancient Egypt, Greece and Byzantium, and gave each zone of the picture its own motif. That is the only way to tell dress, chair and wall apart. Go hunting.

spots.title: Eyes
spots.text: Down the middle of the dress, wide-open eyes set between triangles, a motif taken from ancient Egyptian art. The gown stares back at you.

spots.title: Spirals and discs
spots.text: Coils and coin-like discs crowd around her head and shoulders like a halo. This zone is the back of the armchair she sits in.

spots.title: Red squares
spots.text: The strongest reds in the picture: a block of squares nested inside squares, hard-edged against all the curls nearby.

spots.title: A grey square
spots.text: A square of silvery grey set into the gold of the wall. Small touches like this keep the huge empty left side from going dead.

spots.title: The green floor
spots.text: A strip of plain green under a checkered band. It is the single clue that this golden space is a room, with a floor to stand on.

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: GUSTAV KLIMT in block capitals stacked into a square, with the date split in two below. He designed his name like a stamp.

lesson.text: Did you feel how the eye never settles? It hops from sign to sign and keeps coming back to the face, the one calm and readable thing. That pull between a human being and a dazzling surface is the whole drama of the picture.
Adele is the only person Klimt painted in two full-length portraits. The second one, from 1912, has no gold at all: she stands in a broad black hat against patches of bright color.

Who was she? Born in 1881, the daughter of a banker, married at eighteen. She hosted a salon, a regular gathering at her home where writers, composers and politicians came to talk. Relatives remembered her as frail, sharp and restless, hungry for the education that women of her world were denied. She died of meningitis at forty-three.
Klimt painted a face like a painter and everything around it like a jeweler. The tension between the two is what makes the portrait impossible to forget.

For years a label erased her name. Today the title gives it in full, and the story of the theft is told wherever the painting is shown. The gold used to be the first thing people saw. Now, perhaps, it is the woman.

quiz.question: Why was the portrait shown as “Lady in Gold” in the 1940s?
options: To hide that the sitter was Jewish
Because nobody knew who she was
quiz.explanation: The Nazis had seized the painting and removed Adele's name from it.

quiz.question: Who won the painting back in 2006?
quiz.explanation: Maria Altmann took her claim against Austria all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court.

quiz.question: What is the shimmering background made of?
quiz.explanation: Klimt applied thin sheets of real metal to the canvas.

quiz.question: What did Klimt see in Ravenna in 1903?
quiz.explanation: The ancient gold mosaics of Ravenna fed directly into his Golden Phase.

quiz.question: Which parts of Adele are painted in a lifelike way?
quiz.explanation: Only the skin is modeled realistically. Everything else is flat ornament.

facts.text: Klimt's father worked as a gold engraver.
facts.explanation: Klimt grew up around the craft of working gold.

facts.text: The portrait has always hung in Vienna.
facts.explanation: Since 2006 it has belonged to the Neue Galerie in New York.

facts.text: The whole surface of the painting is covered in gold.
facts.explanation: The skin is painted in oils, and a strip of plain green floor shows at the bottom left.
